# Recommendation: Use `std::sort`

## Short Answer

**Use `std::sort`**. For sorting 10,000,000 uniform `double` values, `std::sort` will almost certainly outperform your custom QuickSort in practice, and it does so with far less effort, better robustness, and comparable or better performance.

## Practical Considerations

### 1. `std::sort` is Introsort, Not Plain QuickSort

C++ standard library implementations use **introsort** — a hybrid algorithm that:
- Starts with QuickSort (for its excellent average-case constant factors and cache behavior)
- Switches to **HeapSort** when recursion depth exceeds `2 * log₂(n)` (guaranteeing O(n log n) worst-case)
- Switches to **InsertionSort** for small subarrays (typically ≤16 elements), eliminating function-call overhead on tiny partitions

Your custom implementation is plain (deterministic-pivot) QuickSort with no fallbacks. This matters in several ways:

| Concern | Your Custom QuickSort | `std::sort` (introsort) |
|---|---|---|
| Worst-case time | O(n²) — e.g., already-sorted input with median pivot can still degrade depending on partition scheme | O(n log n) guaranteed |
| Small-partition overhead | Recursive calls or tail-call optimization via reassignment, but no switching to insertion sort | Cuts off at ~16 elements, uses insertion sort in-place — very cheap for small runs |
| Pivot selection | Always `a[n/2]` — predictable, adversariable, and cache-unfriendly when data has structure | Many implementations use median-of-3 or median-of-9; some shuffle |
